Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Sometimes they say the gears began skipping after a rainy ride. First, I check that the bike is stable and look for obvious damage. Then I squeeze each tire and check the pressure against the number printed on its sidewall. If a tire is soft, I use the floor pump and check again.

I start with the rear wheel because the shifting complaint is at the back. I turn the pedals by hand and move the shifter through each gear. There are three things I check: first, the cable tension; second, whether the derailleur is bent; and third, whether the chain is dirty. I clean the chain with a rag and apply a little bicycle chain lubricant, then I wipe away the extra oil. I don't promise that cleaning will fix every skipped shift. If the cable needs adjusting, I make a small change at the barrel adjuster and test the gears again before the customer leaves. I want to remember the route because the construction fence changes every week, and it is easy to miss the narrow path by the canal. I met Mara and Dev at the bakery on Alder Street just after sunrise. The bakery shutters were still down, but the owner had put a little bowl of water outside for dogs, and two house sparrows were using it like a bath. Mara said she had seen a kestrel over the market roofs on Thursday, but it was too far away to tell if it was carrying anything.

We started at the tram depot instead of the footbridge because a delivery truck was parked across the entrance to the towpath. The depot wall has a painted map of the old streetcar lines, and a young peregrine was perched on the corner above it. Dev spotted the bird first and whispered, “There he is,” but we all looked at the wrong roof for a few seconds. The peregrine stayed still and watched a flock of starlings pass below it. When it turned its head, the sunlight caught the pale cheek and the dark moustache mark. I wrote down nine o’clock, but that was wrong. It was closer to eight forty-five because the clock on the library was running fast by a few minutes.

At the canal, the water was high after Friday rain, and most of the muddy bank was under the surface. We saw three mallards near the floating garden, and one had a blue band on its leg. I could not read the numbers even with the binoculars. There was also a grey heron beside the drain outlet. It held its neck in a tight curve and waited while a cyclist rattled over the metal bridge. Mara said, “Keep watching the feet,” and sure enough, the heron stepped twice, then caught a small fish. I nearly missed it because a bus went by and shook the railing.

1. Route and timing: First, depot wall; then, the canal steps; then, the pocket park behind the clinic; and last, the roof terrace on the library. If the terrace gate is locked, stay on the pavement and check the plane trees from the west side. 2. Meet at eight fifteen at the bakery because the early bus does not run on the usual timetable. 3. Bring binoculars, a pencil, and a warm layer, even if the sky looks clear. The wind comes down the canal and makes the terrace feel colder than the street.

We took the alley to the pocket park and found the little pond covered in duckweed. Someone had left a bright yellow tennis ball on the path, but there was no sign of the dog that owned it. In the plane trees, we heard a wren and then saw it hop along a low branch with its tail held almost upright. Dev thought he heard a blackbird alarm call from the shrubs, though we never located the bird. A woman walking her terrier stopped and asked what we were looking at. Mara told her we were checking the birds, and the woman said, “Oh, then you might like the nest under the cafe awning.” We thanked her but did not go close because the cafe was open and people were moving in and out.

At the library terrace, the gate was open, and a caretaker called Nico let us know the west corner was closed for repairs. He said, “Please keep behind the blue line because one of the paving stones rocks when it rains.” We stayed by the rail and scanned the plane trees below. A pair of wood pigeons were carrying twigs to the fork of a branch, and a ring-necked parakeet flew over with a short, sharp call. I saw a small bird disappear into the ivy but could not identify it. Mara guessed it might be a chiffchaff and then said she was not certain, so I left it as unidentified in my notes rather than decide from one glimpse.

Before we separated, we compared our lists at the bus shelter. Dev had logged twenty-one species, and I had eighteen because I forgot to count the gulls circling above the supermarket roof. Mara had twenty-three and included a jay she saw from the bakery while we were still waiting for coffee. I want to check whether the blue-banded mallard has been reported on the group map and ask the park office if they have a safe way for volunteers to read the band number without disturbing the birds. I also want to bring a small notebook next time because my phone screen was hard to see in the sun.

One last thing: the canal steps were slippery, and the handrail had a loose end near the bottom, so please remind everyone to use the path by the depot wall instead of stepping down to the mud. The heron was still there when we walked back, but the peregrine had left the depot roof, and the starlings were gathering on the wires above Alder Street. It was a good morning, even with the bus noise and the closed corner on the terrace, and I am glad we took the longer route."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-transcribe-0031", "row_sha256": "efae03a569662b3dc04a16aafb01ce73e555f8d2a6597d341b0354fd4ac641c9", "mode": "/transcribe", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Remove true hesitation and accidental restarts. There were nine of us, and Mara had brought the printed route map in a blue folder. The plan was to go through the station plaza, follow the canal path for about half a mile, and finish at the schoolyard garden before the morning traffic got loud. We were not trying to cover every block; we wanted to compare the birds around the water with the ones using the planted courtyards. One person had binoculars but no strap, so Mara reminded him to keep both hands free near the steps and not to set the binoculars on a bench where they could slide off.

At the entrance, we paused beside the bicycle racks and checked the weather on the small display. It said twelve degrees, with light wind from the north and no rain expected until the afternoon. Mara said, “Listen for the first few minutes before looking through binoculars, because a flock can move before you see it.” Well, I thought we would hear mostly pigeons there, but we heard a house sparrow calling from the hedge and a blue jay from somewhere above the station roof. One of the new members asked if the jay was a cardinal, and Mara said, “No, listen to the rough rising call first, and then look for the blue back and white wing bars.” We could not see the bird from the plaza, so she marked it as heard only in her notebook.

We crossed at the signal and took the west side of the canal, where the path is wider. The railing has a loose panel about ten yards past the second lamp, so Mara asked everyone to stay on the paved side and leave room for people on bicycles. A woman with a stroller passed us, and we waited rather than bunch up by the railing. At the water, there were two mallards near the concrete ledge, and one had a pale patch on its head. We wondered whether it was an injury or just a feather pattern, but nobody had a clear view, so Mara said, “Record the pale patch and do not guess.” We also saw a double-crested cormorant drying its wings on the old pump housing. The housing has a green number four painted on the canal side, and that was a useful landmark for the return route.

1. Check the water and the ledges for ducks, cormorants, and gulls.
2. Scan the opposite bank slowly, because birds often sit among the willow roots.
3. Look up at the wires before you move on, because starlings and mourning doves use them.
4. Write down whether you saw or only heard each bird.

That was Mara’s short checklist. We tried it at the narrow bend, where a building blocks part of the sky and a delivery truck was idling across the street. A gull circled once, but we could not identify it beyond “gull,” and two starlings landed on a wire. One member started to call them grackles, then corrected himself and said starlings after he noticed the shorter tails and pale spots. Mara wrote down the correction rather than keeping both guesses.

Near the footbridge, the path splits around a low brick planter. Take the left branch toward the public mural, not the steps that go up to the avenue. We stopped at the bench with the chipped yellow paint because it gives a view of three plane trees and does not block the path. In the nearest tree, a robin was carrying a short, dry twig and flew toward a nest area behind a drainpipe. We did not approach the pipe or try to find the nest. Mara reminded us that a bird carrying material is a useful behavior to note, but the exact nest location should stay out of the public group post. Farther across the canal, we heard what might have been a song sparrow, but the traffic covered the ending of the song, so we left the identification uncertain.

At the mural, we took a five-minute water break and checked that everyone still had the route card. No one needed to leave early, although one person planned to take the number six bus from the schoolyard stop afterward. Mara showed us how she uses a simple note with time, place, species, and behavior instead of writing a long description while the bird is moving. She said a note might read, “7:42, canal planter, robin carrying twig, heading north,” and then a fuller description can be added when there is a safe pause. She also said the phone camera is optional and that people should not step into a cycle lane just to get a photograph. One of us used the phone to record a distant call, but we agreed not to label the sound until we could compare it later.

We continued under the railway bridge, where the light changed and the path surface was damp from overnight cleaning. Slow down under the bridge because the paving stones are uneven and there is a shallow puddle near the drain. We saw a pair of rock pigeons on a beam and a small brown bird that moved into the ivy before anyone could get a good look. One person said it was probably a wren, but Mara asked us to keep it as an unidentified small bird. We listened for another call and heard nothing. The group waited about a minute without stepping off the path, then moved on when a runner approached from behind. At the far side of the bridge, a community garden volunteer was watering two wooden planters and told us that a red-tailed hawk had been seen on the roof earlier that morning. We did not see the hawk ourselves, so Mara put the report in a separate note with the source.

We reached the schoolyard garden at eight twenty and stood outside the low fence rather than entering while the caretaker unlocked the gate. There were three raised beds with winter kale and a row of young serviceberry shrubs by the sidewalk. A house finch called from the nearest shrub, and we watched a squirrel cross the fence but kept it separate from the bird list. Before wrapping up, Mara asked everyone to check their notes for times and spellings and to mark any uncertain identification with a question mark. She said the group would share the route map and a short list of confirmed sightings that evening, but would leave out the possible nest location and the unconfirmed hawk report. The practical route back is the same canal path to the west entrance, and anyone leaving by bus can use the stop on the north side of Alder Street.
